title: Hashing: How a Hash Map Actually Works
oneLiner: A hash map isn't magic O(1) lookup -- it's an array of buckets, a function that turns any key into an index, and a plan for when two keys land on the same bucket.
keyTakeaway: A good hash function spreads keys evenly across buckets, so most lookups touch exactly one bucket -- average O(1). But it's only AVERAGE: a bad hash function (or enough collisions) degrades to checking every key in a bucket one by one, O(n) worst case, which is why Hash Maps: Two Sum's hash map isn't a magic guarantee, just a very good bet.
explanation:
Hash Maps: Two Sum (already in this app) leans on a hash map's near-O(1) lookup without showing HOW that's achieved -- this lesson is the "how." A hash map wraps a plain array of "buckets" (this app starts with 8), plus a HASH FUNCTION that turns any key (a string, a number, anything) into a deterministic (same input, same output, every time) bucket index -- the same key always hashes to the same index, so looking a key up means computing its hash once and going straight to that one bucket, instead of scanning every entry the way a plain array search would have to.

Two different keys can hash to the SAME bucket -- a collision -- and it's not a bug, it's guaranteed to happen eventually for any hash function with more possible keys than buckets (the pigeonhole principle). This table handles it with CHAINING: each bucket holds a small list, and a colliding key just gets appended to whichever bucket it landed in -- looking that key up now means hashing to the bucket, then scanning its (hopefully short) chain. The other common strategy, open addressing/probing, tries a different bucket instead of chaining -- not implemented here, but worth knowing the name exists.

Just like a dynamic array (see Dynamic Arrays: How They Grow), a hash table tracks a LOAD FACTOR -- entries stored divided by bucket count -- and resizes when it gets too full (this table resizes past 0.75), doubling the bucket count and rehashing every existing key into its new bucket, because a key's hash depends on the capacity. That resize is the expensive O(n) operation hiding underneath "hash map insert is O(1)" -- amortized across many inserts, same idea as the dynamic array's amortized O(1) append, and the actual reason both operations get quoted as O(1) despite neither ALWAYS being O(1) on any single call.
